summary: TLS early data exposes requests to replay attacks. This document defines mechanisms for HTTP clients and servers to communicate about requests sent in early data, with techniques for mitigating replay risk.

eli5.summary: Sending a message early is fast, but someone might copy and resend it. This sets up signals so the server can say wait and ask again safely.

questions: what is tls early data in http
what does http status 425 too early mean
subtitle: How HTTP clients, servers and gateways cope with the replay risk of TLS early data, using an Early-Data header and the 425 status code.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 early data lets a client send requests in the first round trip, but an attacker can capture and replay those requests.
tldr.mechanism: Servers can reject early data, delay processing until the handshake completes, or answer 425 (Too Early). The RFC defines the Early-Data request header field and the 425 status code so intermediaries and origin servers can coordinate.
tldr.outcome: Clients may send safe methods in early data and must retry on 425, while gateways must not forward early data to origins that do not understand these signals.

today: RFC 8470 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3).

sections.title: Early Data and the Replay Risk
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 introduces early data, also called zero round-trip time (0-RTT) data. If a client has spoken to the same server recently, it can send data in the first round trip of a connection without waiting for the TLS handshake to finish. For HTTP this avoids the one or two round-trip delays of the handshake, which is a significant performance gain with significant limitations.

The main risk is that an attacker might capture and replay the request or requests. TLS describes techniques that reduce the likelihood of a successful replay, but they can be difficult to deploy and still leave some possibility of attack.

This is different from automated or user-initiated retries: a replay is initiated by an attacker without the client being aware. The advice also applies to 0-RTT in HTTP over QUIC.
sections.eli5: Early data is like handing over your order before you have finished saying hello. It is quick, but a copycat could hand over the same order again.

sections.title: How Early Data Fits into HTTP
sections.content:
Early data is conceptually joined with other application data into one stream. A request can sit entirely in early data or only partly. In a multiplexed protocol such as HTTP/2 or HTTP over QUIC, several requests may be partly delivered in early data.

The model is that once the TLS handshake completes, the early data on that connection is known not to be a replayed copy. That does not mean the data has not been, or will not be, replayed on another connection.
sections.eli5: Once you have properly shaken hands, the server knows your order on this call is real. A copy of it might still have been sent somewhere else.

sections.title: What Servers Do
sections.content:
A server decides whether to offer early data when it sends the TLS session ticket. It has three techniques, which the RFC calls equally effective:

  • Reject early data at the TLS layer. This is all or nothing, so every early request is discarded.
  • Delay processing until after the handshake completes, possibly deciding per request.
  • Answer individual requests with 425 (Too Early) so the client retries without early data.

How much replay risk is tolerable depends on the resource, which only the origin server knows. Method safety is one guide, but some resources have side effects even with safe methods. It is RECOMMENDED that origin servers let resources configure whether early data is appropriate. Without such information, they MUST either reject early data or make sure requests are not processed before the handshake completes.

What matters is when a server starts acting on a request, not whether it was partly early. Parsing header fields without acting on them and determining routing is likely safe. A server can bound memory with the max_early_data_size field of the early_data TLS extension.

Once a server accepts early data it MUST process all requests in it, even if it rejects one with a 425 response. Intermediaries that accept early data MUST implement the signalling mechanism.
sections.eli5: A server can say no to all early orders, make them wait until the hello is done, or tell you to ask again for one particular order.

sections.title: What Clients and Intermediaries Do
sections.content:
A client starts sending HTTP requests immediately after the TLS ClientHello. Absent other information, a client MAY send requests with safe HTTP methods in early data and MUST NOT send unsafe methods, or methods whose safety is unknown, in early data.

If the server rejects early data at the TLS layer, the client MUST start again as if the connection were new, possibly with a different negotiated protocol than the one it used optimistically. Requests sent in early data must be sent again unless the client abandons them. Clients that use early data MUST retry requests on a 425 response.

Automatic retry itself can enable replay. An attacker copies the early data to another server instance that accepts and processes it, then lets the original connection finish. If the client retries, the request is processed twice.

An intermediary MUST NOT use early data when forwarding a request unless early data was used on a previous hop, or it knows the request can be retried safely. Absent better information, that means the request arrived in early data or with the Early-Data header set to 1.
sections.eli5: If you are unsure whether your request could do harm if repeated, wait until the hello is complete. Look-only requests are fine to send early.

sections.title: The Early-Data Header and 425 Status
sections.content:
Two signals let hops coordinate. The Early-Data request header field marks a request that may have been forwarded by an intermediary before its TLS handshake with the client completed. Its only valid value is 1, and its ABNF is Early-Data = "1". An intermediary forwarding before handshake completion MUST add it, MUST NOT remove it, and it MUST NOT appear in a Connection header field, in responses or in request trailers. User agents need not send it. Multiple or invalid instances are treated as a single instance with value 1.

A server cannot make an Early-Data request safe by waiting for the handshake, because it was sent early on a previous hop. If it cannot process it safely, it MUST reject it with 425 (Too Early).

The 425 status code says the server is unwilling to risk processing a request that might be replayed. User agents SHOULD retry automatically, but retries MUST NOT be sent in early data. Intermediaries MUST forward a 425 if the request contained Early-Data. Otherwise an intermediary that received the request in early data MAY retry, but only after the TLS handshake completes. Servers SHOULD NOT emit 425 unless the request came in early data or has Early-Data set to 1. The response is not cacheable by default.
sections.eli5: A sticker saying "this was sent early" travels with the request. A server can reply "too early, try again" and the client asks again after the hello.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Early data exposes a client to replay, and a retried or replayed request can have different side effects. Replays and retries might also support traffic analysis, since a replay may produce a different response whose length is observable even when the content stays confidential.

Gateways. A gateway MUST NOT forward early-data requests unless it knows the origin understands Early-Data and will generate 425 correctly. If unsure, it SHOULD delay forwarding until the handshake finishes or send a 425. A gateway with no supporting origin gains little from early data and should disable it.

Consistency. All server instances, including gateways, must agree to reject or delay a request that is unsafe before handshake completion. Different instances may use different methods and still be consistent. A server MUST NOT act on early data before the handshake completes if another instance could decide differently.

Denial of service. Replaying expensive requests can hurt a server. Under load it SHOULD prefer rejecting early data entirely over selective processing, since 503 or 425 responses often lead to retries and more load.

Out-of-order delivery. In protocols such as QUIC, early data can arrive after the handshake. A server MAY process it then only if it can rely on other instances handling replays correctly.
sections.eli5: The main danger is a copycat repeating your order. Everyone along the way must follow the same rules, and a busy server is better off refusing early orders altogether.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers the Early-Data header field in the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry for protocol http with status standard, and registers status code 425 (Too Early) in the HTTP Status Codes registry.
sections.eli5: The new sticker and the new reply code were added to the official lists so everyone uses the same ones.
